title: The pause
hookLine: revelation pauses, and he grieves, until Ad-Duha and al-Muddaththir come

lines: THE CAVE, THE WORD, THE COMFORT.
cards: After the cave, the command to read, Khadijah's comfort and Waraqa's warning, a person might expect the next message the following night. It doesn't come.
Sahih al-Bukhari ends its account of the first revelation with a short, plain sentence: then the revelation paused for a while. No new verses. No angel at the cave.
Just ordinary days in Mecca, and a man waiting for something he cannot summon. The Arabic word for that gap is today's word.

teach.b: The word is fatrah: a slackening, a lull, a pause. Al-Bukhari's narrations say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was saddened by it.
The sources don't give it a fixed length, and later writers disagree about how long it lasted, so this lesson leaves the number out.
What the reports keep is the feeling and the ending, and readers tell the ending in two ways.

teach.h: THE ANGEL BETWEEN SKY AND EARTH.
teach.b: In one, from Jabir in al-Bukhari, he is walking when he hears a voice, looks up, and sees the same angel from Hira, seated between the sky and the earth. He hurries home, shaking, and asks to be wrapped up.
Then come the opening verses of surah seventy-four, al-Muddaththir, the one wrapped in a cloak.
In Pickthall's translation: "O thou enveloped in thy cloak, Arise and warn!" The pause ends with a job. Another report, from Jundub in al-Bukhari, is one some readers link to the pause.

The Prophet is unwell and doesn't rise for prayer at night, and someone mocks him, saying that whatever used to come to him has abandoned him. Then surah ninety-three comes, ad-Duha, the morning brightness.
Pickthall renders its third verse: "Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee." It answers the mockery almost word for word.

teach.h: THY LORD HATH NOT FORSAKEN THEE.
teach.b: Neither report explains the silence away. It is named, it is felt, and then it ends. Some Muslims turn to ad-Duha in hard seasons, and its next verse promises that what comes later will be better than what came before.

how: Muslims recite surah ad-Duha (93) in prayer and outside it, and some turn to it in hard or uncertain seasons; the pause in revelation is retold in sirah study alongside the first verses at Hira.

o: the cloak he asked to be wrapped in at home
the cave on Hira where the angel first came
the pause in revelation after the first verses

p: the one wrapped in a cloak
the angel between sky and earth

s: the sources agree on exactly how long the pause lasted
the reports don't fix a length, and later writers disagree.
one report has someone mock him, saying what came to him had abandoned him
Jundub's report in al-Bukhari; ad-Duha answers: not forsaken.
the reports pretend the silence was nothing
they say he was saddened by it, and then that it ended.

games.q: you're walking in Mecca after weeks of silence. you hear a voice, look up, and see the angel from Hira between sky and earth. what do you do?
o: stand and ask the angel why it was gone.
hurry home shaking and ask to be wrapped up.
tell no one and carry on walking.
games.why: Jabir's report says he hurried home and asked to be wrapped; then came "arise and warn." the pause ends with a job.

practice: Set in front of you one question you've been holding that hasn't been answered yet, a decision, a prayer, a person. Don't try to solve it; breathe beside it, and let the waiting be what it is without filling it.
If you pray, you can recite ad-Duha, or simply hold its line about not being forsaken.

wordCard.voice: Fatrah. The pause in revelation after the first verses at Hira, ended by the cloak verses and the morning brightness. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a lull or slackening; used for the pause in revelation after the first verses.

carryVoice: Your line: the silence ended. The waiting was part of the story too. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.
